stat_summary: A YouGov survey of people living with a partner or spouse found that 46% of men say taking the bins out is down to them alone and 42% say they do all the gardening, while women lead on almost every indoor chore. Women are up to six times more likely than men to say that only they clean the bathroom and do the laundry; 52% of women say they are the ones who do the dusting; and 27% of men have all their clothes washed by their partner, compared with 1% of women.
stat_source_title: Do men do their fair share of housework?, YouGov

male.headline: Bin Night Warriors: 46 Per Cent of Men Take the Bins Out Alone, and Society Looks the Other Way
male.standfirst: New survey figures confirm what every bloke already knows from a wet pavement in his slippers: men are doing the heavy lifting on bin night, and getting precisely zero thanks for it.
male.image_caption: Martin, 55, just in time, and in slippers.
body_paragraphs: New survey figures have confirmed what every bloke already knows from a wet pavement in his slippers: when it comes to the bins, men are doing the heavy lifting. Among people living with a partner, 46 per cent of men say taking the bins out is down to them alone, and 42 per cent say they do all the gardening. In return, they receive precisely zero thanks, and occasionally a look that says the fox has already been.

“I took both bins down in the rain, in slippers, at ten to twelve, because I’d just remembered the lorry comes at six,” said Martin, 55, from Barnsley. “Nobody threw me a parade. The fox had already been. Nobody even offered me a peg.”

The same YouGov research finds men leading the outdoor jobs and lagging on almost every indoor one, which rather suggests the nation’s unofficial waste-disposal corps is not, as is sometimes claimed, hiding from the hoover. Campaigners are already calling for a National Bin Night Honour, and for a covered walkway to the wheelie bins reserved for men who are, in their words, “just trying to get them out before the lorry”.
Yet where is the outrage? Where is the documentary? Britain’s silent bin-night hero wheels them to the kerb, alone, with only a slightly chewed liner for company.
male.pull_quote: Nobody threw me a parade. The fox had already been. Nobody even offered me a peg.

female.headline: Death by a Thousand Socks: Women Are Up to Six Times More Likely to Do the Laundry Alone, and Experts Say It's No Coincidence
female.standfirst: The same survey has finally exposed the indoor chore crisis gripping British women, and it does not look anything like a quick trip to the kerb.
female.image_caption: Lorraine, 48, ruling on a sock that has, officially, no partner.
body_paragraphs: The same survey has at last exposed the indoor chore crisis gripping British women. They are up to six times more likely than men to say that only they do the laundry and clean the bathroom, and 52 per cent say they are the ones doing the dusting. Twenty-seven per cent of men have all their clothes washed by their partner. For women, that figure is 1 per cent.

“He took the bins out once, in October, and still brings it up,” said Lorraine, 48, from Stockton. “I have done four loads, a bathroom and a sock that has no partner, and nobody’s called me a warrior.”

Researchers – and anyone who has ever turned a school jumper the right way out – will note that the jobs that reset themselves every day land on women, while the bins, heroically, go out once a week. Campaigners are demanding a Laundry Recognition Act and a national apology for the phrase “I’ll just leave these here, they’re not dirty dirty”.
Until then, the country’s unofficial wash-and-fold corps will keep moving, one inside-out school jumper at a time.
female.pull_quote: He took the bins out once, in October, and still brings it up.
